name: NPUs and TPUs
blurb: Purpose-built accelerators outside the GPU line.

items.name: Neural Engine (M-series)
items.note: The NPU in every Apple SoC; the M4 announcement is the canonical spec source for its 38 TOPS on-device engine

items.name: Inferentia
items.note: Amazon's inference-side accelerator, the serving counterpart to Trainium

items.name: Trainium
items.note: Amazon's training chip; Trainium2 UltraServers underpin Anthropic's Project Rainier build-out

items.name: WSE-3
items.note: Wafer-scale engine: one 46,000mm2 die instead of a GPU cluster; 4 trillion transistors

items.name: TPU (Cloud TPU)
items.note: Google's in-house tensor processor family, from Trillium (v6e) onward; trains and serves Gemini and is rentable via Google Cloud

items.name: LPU
items.note: Deterministic single-core-style inference processor; the speed behind the Groq API tracked in the API directory

items.name: Maia 100
items.note: Azure's first in-house AI accelerator, announced with the Cobalt CPU for first-party workloads

reading.body:
Every major cloud provider and device maker now operates its own AI accelerator line, fragmenting the GPU monopoly that once defined AI infrastructure.

The shift from general-purpose GPUs to purpose-built processors reflects a maturation in AI workloads. Training and inference have different bottlenecks. Amazon splits the load between Trainium for training and Inferentia for serving. Google's TPU family handles both, but only internally and through Google Cloud. Apple embeds neural processing into every M-series chip for on-device inference, where power and thermal constraints make generalist hardware wasteful. Cerebras and Groq take different bets: one designs a single massive die to replace an entire cluster, the other optimizes for deterministic, single-pass inference speed.

This diversification matters for compute allocation. If a workload must run on a specific vendor's hardware, it locks teams into that vendor's power budget, data center footprint, and colocation decisions. Google's control over TPU design lets it co-optimize the chip with its cooling and power delivery. Microsoft's Maia entry signals that even owning compute is no longer enough without owning the silicon. The data does not reveal which designs win or which trade-offs between speed, efficiency, and scale actually matter for frontier AI training.

The real constraint this raises is not chip abundance but the buildings and power to run them. A wafer-scale processor like Cerebras solves nothing if there is nowhere to plug it in that can deliver the amperage it demands.
